body.heading: The first gift
paragraphs: Across cultures, naming a child is rarely a private administrative act. In many West African traditions, naming ceremonies gather the community days after the birth to speak the name aloud and welcome its owner. In Iceland, names are traditionally drawn from an approved register rooted in the language. In Greece and other Orthodox and Catholic traditions, a child’s name day — the feast day of their saint — is celebrated much like a birthday, sometimes more.
The variety hides a constant: a name is given in company, because a person is received in company.

body.heading: Names carry cargo
paragraphs: Names arrive carrying grandparents, places, hopes, and occasionally entire philosophies. Learning why someone has their name — asking, listening, remembering the answer — is one of the quickest ways to know a person’s first chapter.
It is also why names deserve care in the small things: pronounced as their owner pronounces them, spelled as they spell them. Getting a name right is respect in its most portable form.

body.heading: Your name, your day
paragraphs: You might adopt the name-day idea without the theology: one day a year, besides a birthday, when each family member gets thanked simply for being who they are, name and all. Children in particular flourish under celebrations that require no achievement at all.
A person’s name is the sound of being known. Celebrate it, and you celebrate the knowing.

takeaway: Ask people about their names, say names correctly, and consider a day that celebrates people for existing.
